3180:
To concatenate means to join or link things together, one after another, forming a single connected chain or sequence.

Think of it like connecting train carriages. Each carriage is a separate unit, but when you link them end-to-end, they all become one long train. That act of linking them together — that is concatenating.

The crucial thing to understand is that concatenation is not just any kind of joining. It is specifically sequential joining — meaning the items are attached in a line, one following the other, in order. The first item comes first, the second comes right after it, the third right after that, and so on.

Imagine three words: "ice", "cream", and "cake".

If you concatenate them, you get: "icecreamcake" — one single result made by joining them end-to-end, in order.

Notice that nothing is mixed or scrambled. The order is preserved. "ice" came first, so it stays first. The items are simply placed one after another to form a single whole.
What Makes It Different from Just "Joining"

You might wonder: isn't this just the same as "joining" or "combining"? Almost — but "concatenate" is more specific in two ways:

1. Order matters. When you concatenate, you are always joining things in a defined sequence. Concatenating A, then B, then C gives you ABC — not BAC or CAB. The sequence is part of the meaning.

2. The items are placed end-to-end. Concatenation is like putting things in a straight line, touching tip-to-tail. It is not about mixing them together (like stirring two liquids), nor about stacking them on top of each other. It is specifically about chaining them in a row.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

In everyday language, concatenate is used (though rarely in casual speech) to describe linking ideas, events, or things in a chain. For example: "A concatenation of unfortunate events led to the disaster." This means one event led to another, which led to another — a chain of connected things in sequence.

In computers and programming, this is where you will encounter the word most often. When programmers talk about concatenating, they almost always mean joining pieces of text (called "strings") end-to-end.

For example:

  • "Hello" + " " + "World" → "Hello World"

You took three separate pieces of text and concatenated them into one. This is one of the most fundamental and frequently performed operations in all of programming. Almost every programming language has a built-in way to do it, and many use symbols like +, &, or . to do so.

In logic and mathematics, concatenating can refer to linking sequences, symbols, or propositions together in a chain to form a longer sequence. The meaning is the same — joining in order, end-to-end.
The Noun Form You Will See

The noun form is concatenation, which refers to the result of concatenating, or the act itself.

  • "The concatenation of those two strings produced a new word."
  • "A concatenation of events."

You will see this noun form at least as often as the verb, so it is worth knowing.

Picture a chain (or a linked list, or train carriages). Concatenate = join links into a chain, in order, end-to-end. The result is always one single connected thing, made from multiple pieces placed sequentially.

To concatenate is to join multiple things together, in sequence, end-to-end, to produce a single connected result. The order of the original items is preserved. Nothing is mixed or rearranged — they are simply lined up and attached to one another. You will see this word most commonly in programming (joining text), but it can apply to any context where things are chained together in a sequence.
3181: Concave means curved inward, like the hollow of a bowl. When a surface or shape is concave, it dips inward rather than bulging outward. Picture holding a bowl right-side up — the inside surface you see is concave. It curves inward, toward a center point.
The word itself hides the clue. Look at con-cave. A cave is a hollow that cuts inward into rock. Concave works the same way — it always describes a surface or shape that curves inward, like a cave.

These two words are almost always learned as a pair because they are exact opposites. Convex means curved outward — like a dome or the outside of a ball, pushing toward you. Concave means curved inward — like the inside of that same ball.

A spoon makes this crystal clear. Flip it face-up and look at the hollow side that holds soup — that is concave. Now flip it over and look at the rounded back that bulges outward — that is convex.

You encounter concave shapes constantly. The inside of a bowl, a cup, or a spoon is concave. A satellite dish curves inward to face the sky. A contact lens is concave on the side that rests against your eyeball. A valley in a landscape dips downward in a concave shape. The inside of a skateboard half-pipe is concave. Even sunken or hollow cheeks on a person are sometimes described as concave.

In geometry, "concave" describes both curves and flat shapes (polygons).

A concave curve bends inward — like the inner edge of a circular arc that curves toward you rather than away from you.

A concave polygon is a flat, closed shape that has at least one inward-pointing "dent." A star shape is a good example — between each outward point of the star, the edges push inward. Those inward corners make it concave. More precisely, a concave polygon has at least one interior angle greater than 180 degrees. There is also a reliable visual test: if you can draw a straight line between any two points on the edge of the shape and that line passes outside the shape, the polygon is concave.

This is where the word appears most often in science, applied to lenses and mirrors.

A concave lens is thinner in the middle than at its edges. Light passing through a concave lens spreads outward, causing the light rays to diverge. This makes things appear smaller. Concave lenses are used in eyeglasses to help people who are nearsighted — people who can see things up close clearly, but struggle to see things far away.

A concave mirror curves inward, like the inside of a bowl. When light hits a concave mirror, it does not scatter — it gets reflected back and focused to a single point called the focal point. This focusing power is extremely useful. Satellite dishes use a concave shape to gather weak signals from space and direct them all to one receiver point. Telescopes use concave mirrors to collect faint starlight from the sky. Car headlights and flashlights use concave reflectors behind the bulb to aim the light forward in a tight, concentrated beam. Makeup and shaving mirrors are slightly concave — they magnify your face because they reflect light in a way that makes the image appear larger and closer than it really is.

"The architect designed a concave roof that curved inward like a bowl." "She used a concave mirror to get a magnified view while applying makeup." "The concave lens in his glasses corrects his nearsightedness." "The canyon formed a vast, concave depression in the earth." "Years of illness had left her cheeks looking hollow and concave."
The single idea that carries you everywhere

No matter what context you encounter "concave" in — science, geometry, architecture, or everyday language — it always means the same thing: curves inward. Whenever you are unsure, just ask yourself: "Does this surface curve inward, into itself?" If yes, it is concave.
3182:
To conceal something means to deliberately hide it — from someone's eyes, from someone's knowledge, or from someone's awareness. When you conceal something, you make sure it is not seen, not found, or not known.

The word works in two directions: hiding something physically (so it can't be seen) and hiding something mentally or informationally (so it can't be known).

She concealed the gift under the bed.
He concealed the truth from his parents.

Both sentences carry the same basic idea — keeping something out of reach of discovery.
The Most Important Feature: It Is Always Deliberate

This is the sharpest and most important thing to understand about "conceal." It is never accidental. When you conceal something, you are making a conscious choice to hide it. There is always intention behind it.

If you forgot to tell someone something, you did not conceal it. But if you chose not to tell them — especially to prevent them from finding out — you concealed it.

This is what makes "conceal" feel slightly more serious and deliberate than a casual word like "hide." It carries a sense of strategy, effort, and purpose.

The word is remarkably flexible. People conceal all kinds of things:

Physical objects — A person can conceal a weapon under their jacket, conceal a letter inside a book, or conceal a key under a doormat. The object is hidden from sight.

Information and facts — A company might conceal its financial losses. A person might conceal their past. A government might conceal evidence. Here, the "hiding" is not physical — it means keeping information from being known or discovered.

Emotions and feelings — This is one of the most common uses. People conceal fear, grief, anger, love, or pain. They don't show it on their face or in their behavior, even though they feel it inside.

She concealed her disappointment behind a smile.

Identity — A person can conceal who they truly are — their real name, their background, their beliefs, or their intentions.

Actions or events — People conceal crimes, mistakes, or affairs. This means they actively work to make sure those things are not discovered.

Concealing does not always mean physically covering something up. It can happen in many ways:

  • By staying silent about something that should be mentioned
  • By lying or telling a half-truth
  • By changing the subject when something gets close to the truth
  • By disguising something so it looks like something else
  • By destroying evidence so nothing can be found
  • By keeping a blank, neutral expression so feelings don't show

All of these are forms of concealment — the common thread is that someone is working to prevent something from being seen or known.

In law: Concealing evidence or concealing a crime is a serious legal offense. It means actively hiding facts that should be disclosed. Courts and legal systems treat concealment as an act of deception with consequences.

In everyday life: People often conceal emotions to be polite, to seem strong, or to protect others from worry. This kind of concealment is very common and not always negative.

In literature and storytelling: Characters frequently conceal their true identity, their secrets, or their motives. This creates mystery, tension, and drama. Many great stories are built around what is being concealed and what happens when it is eventually revealed.

In security and espionage: Agents conceal their identity, conceal information from enemies, or conceal their location. Here, concealing is a strategic act of protection.

Several words are close to "conceal" in meaning, but each has its own shade.

Hide is the most general word. You can hide something without much effort or intention — a child hides behind a curtain during a game. "Conceal" sounds more deliberate, more calculated, and often more serious.

He hid the cookies. (casual, playful)
He concealed the documents from investigators. (serious, intentional)

Disguise means making something look like something else, so it isn't recognized. You disguise something by changing its appearance. Concealing doesn't require a change in appearance — you can conceal something just by keeping it out of sight or out of conversation.

Suppress means stopping something from being expressed or released — you suppress emotions by pushing them down inside yourself. Concealing is broader; it's about hiding from others, whereas suppressing can be something you do even privately, just stopping yourself from feeling or expressing something.

Mask means covering something up so it appears different on the surface — you can mask a bad smell with perfume, or mask nervousness with confidence. "Mask" focuses more on covering the appearance of something, while "conceal" focuses on preventing discovery.

Cover up is the closest informal phrase to "conceal." However, "cover up" often implies a more active or elaborate effort, especially in a negative or scandalous context. You "cover up" a scandal or a crime. "Conceal" is more neutral and can apply to smaller, everyday situations as well.
Sentence Examples to See It in Action

These examples will show you how the word behaves in real usage:

  • The suspect tried to conceal his identity by wearing a hood.
  • She worked hard to conceal her excitement until the right moment.
  • The report revealed that the company had concealed its losses for years.
  • He could not conceal his anger — it showed on his face.
  • The spy carefully concealed the document inside a hollow pen.
  • Doctors discovered she had been concealing symptoms for months.
  • The truth can only be concealed for so long before it comes out.

Notice how naturally the word fits physical hiding, emotional hiding, and informational hiding equally well.

Since you want a complete understanding, here are the other forms of this word:

Concealed (adjective/past tense) — something that has been hidden. "A concealed weapon." "He concealed his past."

Concealing (present participle) — the ongoing act of hiding. "She was concealing her true feelings."

Concealment (noun) — the act or state of hiding something. "The concealment of evidence is a crime."

Concealer (noun) — a person who conceals, or a cosmetic product used to hide blemishes on skin.

The direct opposite of "conceal" is reveal — to make something known or visible that was previously hidden. Other opposites include disclose (formally reveal), expose (reveal something unwanted or hidden), and uncover (discover something that was concealed).
A Final Way to Remember It

If you want one clean mental anchor: to conceal = to keep hidden on purpose.

It can be an object, a feeling, a fact, or an identity. It always involves a choice. And the concealed thing, by definition, is something someone did not want found.
3183:
To concede means to admit or give up something, even when you don't want to. The most important feeling hiding inside this word is reluctance — you're not happily agreeing or freely giving. You're doing it because the situation has forced you to, because the facts are too strong to deny, or because continuing to resist no longer makes sense.

That reluctant, against-your-own-interest quality is what makes "concede" precise and powerful. It's not just admitting or giving up — it's doing so from a position where you wished things were different.

1. Conceding in Thought or Argument — "I admit this is true"

When you concede a point, you acknowledge that something is true or valid, even though it works against your own position or argument.

Imagine you and a friend are arguing. You've been insisting that a certain movie was released in 2005. Your friend shows you proof it was 2007. You say, "Fine, I concede — you're right." You're not changing your whole opinion about the movie. You're simply accepting that on this specific point, you were wrong.

This is the most common everyday use of the word. Notice:

  • You don't have to agree with everything, just the specific thing you're conceding.
  • A good debater sometimes concedes a minor point to strengthen their overall argument — they are saying, "Yes, that small thing is true, but here's why my bigger point still stands."
  • You can say "I concede that..." followed by the thing you are admitting: "I concede that the process was flawed, but the final result was still correct."

2. Conceding in Competition or Conflict — "I give this up to you"

When you concede in a competition, a negotiation, a war, or an election, you are surrendering something — a claim, a victory, a territory, a privilege — to the other side.

A few vivid examples:

  • A politician who concedes an election is publicly announcing that they accept they have lost. They are giving up their claim to the win. This is called conceding defeat.
  • In chess, a player concedes when they tip over their king — they are handing the victory to their opponent rather than playing to the bitter end.
  • In a peace negotiation, a country might concede territory — it gives up land to the other side as part of an agreement.
  • In soccer and other sports, a team concedes a goal when the opposing team scores. The team didn't want to let that goal in — it was forced upon them. This usage is especially common in British English.

Conceding is not the same as freely agreeing or voluntarily giving.
If you happily hand your friend a gift, you didn't concede it to them. But if you've been arguing over who deserves the last slice of pizza, and the evidence piles up against you, and you finally say "Alright, it's yours" — that's a concession.

Conceding is not the same as total surrender.
You can concede one thing while still holding your ground on everything else. A lawyer in a courtroom might concede that the defendant was present at the scene, but still argue the defendant is not guilty. Conceding one point does not mean losing the whole argument.

Conceding can be a sign of strength, not weakness.
Wise negotiators, lawyers, and thinkers often strategically concede minor points. It builds trust, shows intellectual honesty, and lets them focus their energy on the bigger battle. Refusing to ever concede anything — even the obviously true — makes you look unreasonable.

Notice the different grammatical patterns:

  • Concede + that (clause): "She conceded that the plan had some weaknesses." (admitting something is true)
  • Concede + noun: "He conceded defeat gracefully." / "The team conceded three goals." (giving something up or allowing something)
  • Concede + something + to someone: "They conceded the northern regions to the opposing army." (surrendering something to a specific party)
  • Concede to (someone/something): "He eventually conceded to her demands." (yielding to pressure or a request)

Since you'll encounter similar words, here's how they differ:

Admit is broader and more neutral. You admit a fact, a mistake, or a feeling. There's no necessary sense of giving something up to an opponent. "I admit I was nervous" — there's no competition here. Concede carries a stronger sense of a position or claim being given up to someone else.

Acknowledge is even more neutral — it simply means recognizing that something exists or is true, with no reluctance required at all. "She acknowledged the applause."

Yield focuses on giving way — stepping back, letting someone else pass or take precedence. It's physically and metaphorically about making room. Concede is about admitting or surrendering a specific point, right, or victory.

Surrender is more total and dramatic — it usually means giving up completely, often in a conflict. Conceding can be partial. You concede a point or a goal; you surrender everything.

To concede is to admit something is true or to give something up to another person — reluctantly, and usually because the facts, the situation, or the power of the moment has left you no better option.
3184: "Conceit" has two completely separate meanings that are used in different contexts. One is everyday, and one is literary. Understanding both will give you the full picture.
Meaning 1: An Inflated, Unrealistic Opinion of Yourself

This is the meaning you're most likely to encounter in daily life.

When someone has conceit, it means they think they are far more talented, intelligent, attractive, or important than they actually are. It goes beyond ordinary confidence. A confident person believes in themselves based on honest self-awareness. A person full of conceit has puffed up their own image in their mind — they are in love with themselves, and it shows.

Think of it this way: confidence says "I am good at this." Conceit says "I am the best, and everyone else is lesser."

Examples in use:

  • "His conceit was astonishing — he truly believed no one in the room was as smart as him."
  • "She had the talent, but her conceit drove away everyone who could have helped her."

The key adjective to know: Someone who has conceit is described as conceited. If someone calls you conceited, they mean you are arrogantly, unrealistically full of yourself. "Conceit" is the state; "conceited" is the quality.

Shades and nuance: Conceit carries a slightly old-fashioned and literary feel compared to the more casual word "arrogance." Arrogance often feels loud and aggressive — the arrogant person asserts their superiority. Conceit is more internal and self-absorbed — the conceited person is simply besotted with themselves. They may not even bother to attack others; they're too busy admiring themselves. It also overlaps with vanity, but vanity tends to focus specifically on physical appearance, while conceit is broader — it can apply to intelligence, skill, status, or any quality a person might overvalue in themselves.
Meaning 2: A Literary Device — An Elaborate, Surprising Comparison

This meaning lives in the world of literature and poetry, and it is completely unrelated to pride.

In writing — especially in poetry — a conceit is an extended and surprising comparison between two things that, at first glance, seem to have absolutely nothing in common. The writer takes an unexpected connection and stretches it out, develops it in detail, and makes it the backbone of the poem or passage. It's not a quick one-line simile. It's a comparison that the writer commits to, explores from multiple angles, and sustains throughout a piece of writing.

The key qualities of a conceit are:

  • It is surprising — you would not naturally think to compare these two things
  • It is clever and intellectual — it makes you think
  • It is extended — it is not just a flash of comparison but a developed, detailed argument built on that comparison

A famous example: The poet John Donne, in his poem "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning," compares two lovers — one about to go on a journey, one staying behind — to the two legs of a drawing compass (the instrument used to draw circles). This seems bizarre at first. What do lovers have to do with a compass? But Donne develops it fully: just as a compass has two legs joined at the top, the two lovers are spiritually joined. When one leg moves outward (one lover travels), the other leg (the one staying) leans toward it, remains anchored, and enables the moving leg to complete its circle and return to where it started. The further out one leg goes, the more the other leans with it. Donne uses every detail of how a compass actually works to describe the relationship between the lovers. That sustained, unlikely, intellectually worked-out comparison — that is a conceit.

The Two Types of Conceit You Should Know

1. The Petrarchan Conceit
Named after the Italian poet Petrarch, this type of conceit uses comparisons that, while elaborately developed, are conventional in love poetry — meaning they were used so often they became clichés. Comparing a woman's eyes to stars, her lips to red roses, her skin to snow, or her hair to rivers of gold — these are Petrarchan conceits. They were once considered beautiful and elevated, but over time they became so predictable that later writers mocked them. When Shakespeare wrote "My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun," he was deliberately pushing back against Petrarchan conceits.

2. The Metaphysical Conceit
This is the more intellectually daring and celebrated type. Associated with the Metaphysical poets of the 17th century (John Donne, George Herbert, Andrew Marvell), the metaphysical conceit reaches for shocking, unexpected, and often scientific or philosophical comparisons. The compass example above is a metaphysical conceit. These comparisons feel almost wrong at first — and then, as the poet develops them, they feel startlingly right. That tension between initial surprise and eventual sense is the hallmark of the metaphysical conceit.

Meaning 1Meaning 2

When you see "conceit" in an everyday sentence about a person's character or behavior, it means vanity and an inflated self-image.

When you see "conceit" in a sentence about a poem, a novel, a play, or writing in general, it means an extended, clever, and surprising comparison that structures a piece of writing.

These two meanings share the same word but nothing else. The literary term does not come from the idea of being proud; they simply evolved in the same language and arrived at the same spelling.

One final test to cement your understanding:

  • "His conceit made it impossible to work with him." → Pride. He thought too highly of himself.
  • "The central conceit of the poem is comparing grief to a slow tide coming in." → Literary device. The comparison between grief and a tide is the clever, extended metaphor that drives the poem.

Now you know everything there is to know about the noun "conceit" — both where it lives in daily life and where it lives in literature.
3185:
When we say someone is conceited, we mean they have an excessively high opinion of themselves — of their looks, intelligence, talent, or importance — and they make sure others around them know it. It is always a negative word. Nobody uses "conceited" as a compliment.

Think of it this way: a conceited person looks in the mirror and thinks, "I am truly exceptional — smarter, better-looking, or more talented than the people around me." And then they act on that belief, often in ways that make others feel small, ignored, or irritated.
What It Looks Like in Real Life

Conceit is not just an inner feeling — it spills outward into a person's behavior. A conceited person tends to:

  • Talk about themselves constantly, steering every conversation back to their own achievements, appearance, or opinions.
  • Fish for compliments, or simply assume compliments are always deserved.
  • Dismiss or belittle other people's ideas, work, or abilities, because deep down they believe nobody else measures up to them.
  • React poorly to criticism, because a truly conceited person cannot accept that they might be wrong or flawed.
  • Expect to be noticed, admired, and treated as special — and feel genuinely puzzled or offended when they are not.
A Key Distinction: Conceited vs. Confident

This is where most learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Confidence is a healthy belief in your own abilities. A confident person thinks, "I can do this. I am good at this." They don't need to put others down. They don't constantly talk about how great they are. They just quietly trust themselves.

Conceit is confidence that has gone too far and turned sour. A conceited person doesn't just believe in themselves — they believe they are superior to others, and they want recognition for it. The moment someone starts measuring their own worth by making others feel lesser, confidence has crossed the line into conceit.

Here is a simple test: A confident person lifts a room. A conceited person shrinks it.

These will help you see the word working in natural contexts:

  • "He is so conceited that he spent the entire dinner talking about his own achievements without once asking anyone else a question."
  • "She rejected every suggestion from her teammates — her conceited attitude made it impossible for anyone to work with her."
  • "Don't be put off by how conceited he seems at first; he genuinely believes he is the most talented person in any room he walks into."
  • "The young actor became conceited after his first success, and soon nobody on set could stand being around him."
The Feeling It Creates in Others

When you are around a conceited person, you tend to feel one or more of these things: annoyed, invisible, undervalued, or just plain tired. Conceited people drain the energy of those around them because the interaction is always one-sided — it is always about them.

Not all conceited people behave in extreme ways. Conceit exists on a spectrum.

On the mild end, someone might be slightly self-absorbed, casually assuming they are right about everything, or a little too eager to talk about their own successes. You might think, "They are a bit full of themselves," but you can still get along with them.

On the strong end, a person's conceit can make them genuinely cruel — dismissing others, taking credit for others' work, or humiliating people who challenge them. This is where conceit gets very close to arrogance.
How Conceited Differs from Similar Words

Understanding nearby words will sharpen your grasp of this one.

Arrogant and conceited are cousins, but arrogance carries a more aggressive edge. An arrogant person doesn't just think highly of themselves — they actively look down on others with a kind of contempt. Conceit is more about self-obsession and the hunger for admiration; arrogance is more about dominance and dismissal. A conceited person wants to be adored. An arrogant person doesn't particularly care if you adore them — they just think you are beneath them. In practice, many people are both.

Vain is another close relative, but vanity is almost always tied specifically to physical appearance. A vain person is obsessed with how they look — always checking their reflection, obsessing over their style, and fishing for compliments about their beauty. A conceited person may or may not be vain, because their excessive self-regard can be about intellect, talent, or status — not just looks. Vanity is a type of conceit, but conceit is the broader word.

Proud is importantly different. Pride is not a bad thing on its own. You can be proud of your child, proud of a job well done, proud of your culture — that is healthy and human. Conceited is always negative. A proud person celebrates something genuinely worth celebrating. A conceited person inflates their own worth beyond what is real or deserved.

Narcissistic is the most extreme version and carries a clinical weight. Narcissism (as a personality trait) involves a deep, rigid pattern of grandiosity, a lack of empathy, and an intense need for admiration — it goes much deeper than everyday conceit. You might casually call someone conceited after a single irritating conversation. You would only call someone narcissistic after observing a consistent, deeply rooted pattern of behavior.
Can a Person Be Conceited Without Realising It?

Yes — and this is one of the more interesting things about the word. Some conceited people are fully aware of their own high self-regard and wear it almost like a badge. But many conceited people have no idea how they come across. They genuinely believe they are simply being honest about their own greatness, not realising that their behavior is off-putting or hurtful to others. This is part of why conceit is so frustrating to deal with — the person causing the problem is often the last one to see it.
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine a peacock spreading its feathers in front of everyone, not because it needs to, but simply because it cannot help showing off how beautiful it believes itself to be — and because it expects everyone to stop and stare in admiration.

That peacock is conceited.
3186:
Something is conceivable if the human mind is capable of imagining it, picturing it, or accepting that it might exist or happen — even if it hasn't happened, isn't happening, and may never happen. It is about what is possible in the realm of thought, not necessarily what is real or certain.

A simple way to feel it: "Can I picture this? Can my mind accept this as a possibility?" If yes, it is conceivable.

The word is built on the idea of conceiving — which in its mental sense means to form an idea or picture of something in your mind. So, conceivable simply means "able to be conceived (thought of) in the mind."

Notice that this is very different from saying something is true, likely, or even possible in real life. Conceivable is only asking one question: can you think of it? Can your mind form that idea at all?

For example, a fire-breathing horse is conceivable — you just imagined one. It doesn't exist, but your mind had no trouble picturing it. That's the threshold conceivable requires: mental availability, nothing more.

This is crucial. When you say something is conceivable, you are making a very modest claim. You are not saying:

  • It is true.
  • It is likely.
  • It is realistic or reasonable.
  • It will happen.

You are only saying: "It can be imagined. It can be entertained as an idea. I can't rule it out completely."

This is why "conceivable" often carries a cautious, careful tone. When someone says "It is conceivable that he lied," they aren't accusing anyone. They are simply saying: "I can picture it. I can't say it's impossible."
How It Sits Among Similar Words

Think of these words on a scale of confidence, from weakest to strongest:

Conceivable → Possible → Plausible → Likely → Certain

Conceivable is at the weak end. It only means the imagination can reach something. Possible is slightly stronger — it means something could realistically happen. Plausible is stronger still — it means something seems reasonable and believable. Likely means it will probably happen. Certain means it definitely will.

So if something is conceivable, it may not even be possible in the real world — it just has to be imaginable. And if something is possible, it is almost always conceivable too, because real possibilities are easy to imagine.

Compare:

  • "A dragon is conceivable." — Yes, you can picture one. But it isn't possible in our world.
  • "Rain tomorrow is possible." — This is stronger. It means it could actually happen.

Conceivable and imaginable are very close in meaning and can often be swapped. If there is any difference, "imaginable" leans more toward the picture in your mind, while "conceivable" leans slightly more toward the idea being accepted as within the bounds of what might be true or real — but in everyday use, they're nearly identical.

Pattern 1: "It is conceivable that..."

This is the most common structure. It introduces a possibility you're not sure about, but you're willing to entertain.

  • "It is conceivable that scientists will find a cure within ten years." (= I can imagine it happening; I'm not ruling it out.)
  • "It is conceivable that she didn't receive the message." (= I can picture that being true; it's a possibility.)

Pattern 2: "Every conceivable [noun]"

Here, "conceivable" means "that can be thought of" — so "every conceivable option" means every option you could possibly think of. This pattern is used to express completeness or exhaustiveness.

  • "The team tried every conceivable method to solve the problem." (= They tried all methods anyone could think of.)
  • "The store sells every conceivable type of coffee." (= You can find any type of coffee you could imagine there.)

Pattern 3: "The only conceivable [noun]"

Used to say that, among all things you could think of, only one stands out.

  • "The only conceivable explanation is that the package was lost." (= If I try to think of all possible explanations, only one comes to mind.)

Pattern 4: "Barely conceivable" or "scarcely conceivable"

This means something is so difficult to imagine that your mind can only just barely form the idea.

  • "It is barely conceivable that anyone could survive that accident." (= It's almost impossible to imagine, but not fully impossible.)

The opposite of conceivable is inconceivable, meaning impossible to imagine or believe — completely beyond what the mind can picture or accept.

  • "It was inconceivable to them that they could lose the match." (= They couldn't even picture losing. It was beyond imagination.)
  • "The scale of the destruction was almost inconceivable." (= So enormous that the mind struggles to fully picture it.)

Note the word "almost" in the second example. People often soften "inconceivable" with words like "almost" or "nearly" when something is merely very hard to imagine, rather than truly impossible to imagine.

"Conceivable" is a fairly formal word. You'll find it more in writing, professional conversation, and careful speech than in casual everyday talk. In casual conversation, people might just say "possible" or "imaginable" or simply "I can imagine that."

It also frequently appears in negative or questioning contexts, as people use it to probe the outer edges of what might be true:

  • "Is it even conceivable that no one noticed?"
  • "There is no conceivable reason for his behaviour."

These two can feel similar but they're different. Conceivable asks: Can I picture it? Believable asks: Can I accept it as true or realistic? Something can be conceivable (imaginable) but not believable (too far-fetched to accept). For example, "A human living to 300 years old is conceivable but not believable with current science."

Conceivable describes something that the mind is capable of imagining, picturing, or entertaining as a possibility — regardless of whether it is true, likely, or even realistic. It is one of the weakest claims you can make about a possibility: you are only saying the idea can be formed. It contrasts with impossible to imagine (inconceivable) and falls below possible, plausible, and likely on the scale of certainty. It appears most often in the patterns "it is conceivable that...," "every conceivable...," and "the only conceivable...," and its closest synonym is imaginable.
3187:
"Conceivably" means "in a way that is possible to imagine."

When you say something is conceivable, you mean your mind can picture it happening — it's not impossible. So when you say "conceivably," you're saying: "I can imagine this being true or possible, even if I'm not certain."

The root idea here is conceiving — not in the sense of having a baby, but in the older sense: forming an idea in your mind. To conceive of something means to be able to picture it mentally.

So "conceivably" = "in a way that the mind can picture as possible."

This is a word of cautious possibility. It sits in the space between "this will definitely happen" and "this is impossible." When someone uses it, they're essentially saying:

"I'm not promising this, but I can imagine it being true."

It's honest and careful. It doesn't overclaim. It signals that the speaker is opening a door of possibility, but not fully walking through it.

Here are several examples across different situations, with explanations:

Example 1:

"This could conceivably be the best film made in the last decade."

What it means: The speaker isn't declaring it the best film — they're saying "I can imagine making the case that it is." It's praise, but tempered with intellectual humility.

Example 2:

"If the train is delayed, we could conceivably miss the entire first half."

What it means: Missing the first half isn't certain, but it's a real possibility the speaker can picture. The word warns without panicking.

Example 3:

"He could conceivably win the election, but it would take a lot of things going his way."

What it means: A win isn't predicted — it's just within the range of imagination. Often this kind of sentence implies the possibility is surprising or unlikely, but not impossible.

Example 4:

"How could anyone conceivably believe that?"

What it means: This is a rhetorical use — the speaker is saying it's hard to even imagine believing something. Here "conceivably" is used to express disbelief or incredulity.
A Key Nuance: It Often Implies "Even If Unlikely"

This is subtle but important. Compare:

  • "It's possibly raining in Mumbai." → Neutral statement of possibility.
  • "It could conceivably snow in Mumbai." → The possibility exists, but it's unusual. The word conceivably here subtly signals: "Yes, I can imagine it, but I'm aware it's a stretch."

So "conceivably" often carries a slight implication that the possibility is at the outer edge of what seems realistic. It acknowledges something could happen while hinting that it might require a bit of imagination to believe.

This makes it more vivid than "possibly." It says: "I had to actually picture this in my mind to arrive at it."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Possibly:
More neutral. Just says something might happen. No suggestion that it requires imagination.

"It will possibly rain today." (straightforward, weather-based probability)

Conceivably:
More imaginative. Suggests the speaker actively pictured it and found it within the range of possibility, perhaps against their initial instinct.

"It could conceivably snow in Chennai in December." (possible, but requires effort to picture)

Theoretically:
Based on logic or rules, not necessarily on imagination. If the rules don't prevent something, it's "theoretically" possible.

"Theoretically, you could drive from Delhi to London." (the logic works, the physics allow it — but practically, no.)

Conceivably is warmer and more human than theoretically. It's about the imagination, not just logic.

Imaginably:
Very similar to conceivably, but rarer. "Conceivably" is the more natural, common choice in modern English.

You'll almost always see "conceivably" in sentences that also use modal verbs like could, might, may, can:

  • "This could conceivably work."
  • "She might conceivably agree to it."
  • "He can conceivably finish by Friday."

It rarely stands alone or starts a sentence. It lives inside a sentence, usually right after a modal verb or the word "not":

  • "I cannot conceivably understand why he did that." (= I can't even imagine understanding it)

"Conceivably" is a slightly formal or careful word. You'll hear it in:

  • Journalism and analysis ("This policy could conceivably affect millions.")
  • Academic or professional writing
  • Careful, thoughtful speech

In casual conversation, people might just say "maybe" or "possibly." But when someone says "conceivably," they usually want to sound more precise — they're being deliberate about the kind of possibility they mean.

What it meansIn a way that is possible to imagine
What it signalsCautious possibility; "I can picture this being true, but I'm not certain"
Hidden toneOften implies the possibility is surprising or at the edge of likelihood
Closest synonymPossibly — but with a more imaginative, slightly more vivid flavor
Typical companyModal verbs: could, might, may, can

The word is essentially your mind's way of keeping doors open. When you say something is conceivable, you're not predicting it — you're simply refusing to rule it out. And conceivably, as the adverb, is the word you use to wear that careful, honest uncertainty on your sleeve.
3188: "Conceive" always refers to the moment something begins to exist — either in your mind, or in the body. Whether it's an idea, a vision, or a new life, conceiving is the act of bringing something into existence for the very first time. Keep this thread in mind, and every meaning will feel natural.
Meaning 1: To Form an Idea or Plan in Your Mind

This is the most common use of the word. When you conceive something — an idea, a plan, a story, a theory — you are the one who creates it in your mind for the first time. You are the originator. The idea didn't exist before, and now it does, because of you.

"She conceived the idea for the novel while sitting on a train."
"The scientist conceived a new theory about the universe."
"The project was originally conceived as a small, local experiment."

Notice that conceiving isn't the same as just thinking about something randomly. It's that specific, creative moment — the birth of an idea. It carries a sense of originality and invention.
Meaning 2: To Imagine or Picture Something (often used with "of")

This is closely related to Meaning 1, but here you are not creating something new — you are trying to form a mental picture of something that already exists or is being described. This is especially used for things that are hard to wrap your mind around — things that are too large, too extreme, too abstract, or too unfamiliar.

This form is very commonly used in negative sentences.

"I cannot conceive of a world without compassion."
"Can you conceive of the true scale of the universe?"
"She couldn't conceive how anyone could be so cruel."
"The suffering was too great to conceive."

When you say "I cannot conceive of it," you're saying: "My mind simply cannot form an image of it — it's beyond what I can imagine."
Meaning 3: To Think of Something in a Particular Way

"Conceive of" can also mean to hold a specific understanding or mental model of something — to see it in a certain light or framework. Here, you're not saying the thing is hard to imagine; you're describing how someone understands or defines something.

"He conceived of success as freedom, not wealth."
"Different cultures conceive of time very differently."
"Early scientists conceived of the brain as a kind of machine."

In simple words: how you conceive of something = how you fundamentally understand or think about it.

In biology and medicine, conceive refers to the moment a sperm fertilizes an egg and pregnancy begins. This moment is called conception. The subject of the sentence is typically the woman, or sometimes the couple together.

"She conceived in January and gave birth in October."
"The couple had been trying to conceive for two years."
"The baby was conceived through IVF treatment."

This meaning is the most literal and physical version of the same core idea — something (a new life) begins to exist.
Grammar: How to Use "Conceive" in a Sentence

Understanding the grammar patterns will help you use this word correctly.

Pattern 1 — conceive + noun (conceive takes a direct object):

"She conceived a plan." / "He conceived a brilliant idea."

Pattern 2 — conceive of + noun:

"I can't conceive of such cruelty." / "They conceived of a new approach."

Pattern 3 — conceive that + clause:

"I cannot conceive that he would lie to us."
"It is hard to conceive that this was all built by hand."

Pattern 4 — conceive of + noun + as + noun/adjective (to think of X as Y):

"She conceived of the city as a living, breathing organism."
"He conceived of his role as a guardian, not a ruler."

Pattern 5 — Passive voice (very common in formal or written English):

"The project was conceived in 2015."
"The plan was originally conceived as a temporary measure."
The Word Family: Related Words You'll Encounter

Learning the word family of "conceive" will make you much stronger with this word.

Conception (noun) — has three uses that mirror the verb:

  • The birth or formation of an idea: "The conception of this project took months of brainstorming."
  • A person's understanding or idea of what something is: "Her conception of justice is very different from mine."
  • The biological beginning of pregnancy: "Conception occurs when a sperm fertilizes an egg."

Concept (noun) — a general idea or mental framework for something. It is directly linked to the intellectual meaning of "conceive."

"Gravity is a scientific concept."

Conceivable (adjective) — something that can be imagined or is possible to think of:

"It is conceivable that he simply forgot."
"Every conceivable option was explored before a decision was made."

Inconceivable (adjective) — something impossible to imagine, often used to express shock or disbelief:

"The scale of destruction was inconceivable."
"It seemed inconceivable that no one had noticed."

Conceivably (adverb) — meaning "possibly" or "it can be imagined that":

"This could conceivably take several years."
"He might conceivably change his mind."

Here is the elegant truth about this word: all of its meanings are about the beginning of something.

  • When an idea is born in your mind → you conceived it.
  • When something is too big for your mind to even begin to form → you cannot conceive of it.
  • When a new life begins in the body → a baby is conceived.

The word always sits right at that starting point — the moment of origin, the moment of first existence. Once you see that, the word will never feel confusing again.
3189:
Before looking at the individual meanings, it helps to understand the single idea that runs through all of them.

Imagine a magnifying glass on a sunny day. Sunlight falls everywhere — on grass, on trees, on the whole field. But when you hold the lens over a piece of paper, something changes. All that scattered light gets pulled inward and pushed into one tiny, burning point. That point is so powerful it can start a fire, even though the sunlight was harmless when it was spread out.

That image captures the soul of "concentrate":

To take something that is spread out, scattered, or weak — and bring it together into one focused point, one place, or one stronger form.

Everything else about this word grows from that root idea.
Meaning 1: To Direct All Your Attention Onto One Thing

This is the most common, everyday use of the word.

When you concentrate on something, you aim your full mental energy at it. Your mind stops jumping from thought to thought. Distractions fade out. You are fully locked in on one thing.

Examples:

  • "Stop talking — I'm trying to concentrate."
  • "She concentrated on the exam paper and didn't look up once."
  • "It's very hard to concentrate when you're exhausted."
  • "He concentrated all his mental energy on solving the problem."

The key preposition: You concentrate on something. This is the standard pattern. "Concentrate on your work." "Concentrate on what I'm saying."

An important nuance: Concentrating is a choice. You deliberately pull your mind inward and hold it in one place. The opposite happens when something distracts you — your attention scatters outward again, and you lose concentration. This is why people say "I can't concentrate" when there is noise or chaos around them. The mind is being pulled in too many directions at once.

Degrees matter here. You can concentrate a little (mildly focused) or concentrate deeply (so absorbed that you don't even notice time passing). When someone is extremely concentrated, they are sometimes described as being in a state of deep focus — the world around them almost disappears.
Meaning 2: To Gather or Collect Things Into One Place

Here, the word shifts from mental focus to physical or geographical gathering. When things concentrate in a place, they come together there instead of being spread out evenly.

Examples:

  • "The general concentrated his troops at the northern border." → He moved all the soldiers from different regions into one location.
  • "Wealth is concentrated in a few large cities." → Most of the money is not spread evenly across the country; it pools in certain places.
  • "Power was concentrated in the hands of one person." → Control, which could have been shared among many, was pulled together and held by one.
  • "The company concentrated all its operations in one building."

Notice that in these examples, something that could have been scattered or shared is instead pulled to one point. This can be done intentionally (the general moves troops) or it can be a natural result over time (wealth slowly pools in cities).
Meaning 3: To Make a Substance Stronger by Removing What Weakens It

This meaning is very common in cooking, science, chemistry, and industry.

When you concentrate a liquid, you remove water (or another diluting substance) from it. What remains behind is thicker, stronger, and more powerful — because the same amount of active material is now packed into a smaller volume.

Examples:

  • "Boil the soup for 30 minutes to concentrate the flavors." → As water evaporates, the remaining soup carries stronger, richer taste.
  • "The factory concentrates orange juice by removing most of the water." → That is why "concentrated orange juice" is thick and syrupy — you are supposed to add water back before drinking it.
  • "The chemist concentrated the acid solution." → Made it more potent by reducing the diluting liquid.

A simple way to picture this: Imagine making tea. One teabag in a full cup gives you weak tea. One teabag in a tiny cup gives you something strong and intense. The tea itself hasn't changed — but it's been concentrated into a smaller space, so it feels more powerful.

The key idea: less space + same amount of active substance = more concentrated = stronger.
Meaning 4: To Direct or Channel Energy, Force, or Light Toward a Single Point

This meaning applies when something like light, heat, sound, or physical force is focused and aimed precisely, instead of being allowed to spread in all directions.

Examples:

  • "A lens concentrates sunlight into a single point." → Light rays that were spreading out in all directions are aimed at one tiny spot.
  • "The parabolic dish concentrates the incoming signal."
  • "The boxer concentrated every ounce of his strength into that one punch."
  • "Solar panels concentrate energy from a large surface into a single output."

This is essentially the magnifying glass image from the beginning — used literally in science and physics.

Concentrate without an object (intransitive):
Here, the word stands alone and describes the act of focusing one's mind.

  • "I just can't concentrate right now."
  • "She sat quietly and tried to concentrate."

Concentrate + object (transitive):
Here, something specific is being gathered, directed, or strengthened.

  • "Concentrate your attention on the task."
  • "They concentrated the workforce in one city."
  • "Heat concentrates the flavor."

Concentrate on + something:
When talking about mental focus, "on" is almost always needed.

  • ✅ "Concentrate on your breathing."
  • ❌ "Concentrate your breathing." (This doesn't work for mental focus)

Passive form — "is/was concentrated":
When you want to describe where something has ended up being gathered, you use the passive.

  • "Most of the country's wealth is concentrated in the capital."
  • "Authority was concentrated at the top of the organization."
  • "Flavor is concentrated in the skin of the fruit."
The Thread That Connects Every Meaning

Every single use of "concentrate" carries one underlying logic:

Something scattered, spread, or diluted → pulled inward → becomes more focused, more gathered, or more powerful.

Your attention is scattered across ten things → you concentrate → all of it points at one thing.
Soldiers are spread across a country → they concentrate → all of them are at one border.
Juice is mostly water → you concentrate it → the water leaves, the flavor stays and strengthens.
Sunlight spreads in all directions → a lens concentrates it → one burning point.

The magnifying glass is always there, doing the same thing, no matter what is being concentrated.
What It Means to Not Concentrate

Understanding a word's opposite can sharpen your sense of it.

When attention is not concentrated, it is scattered or distracted — pulled in many directions at once.
When people or things are not concentrated, they are dispersed or spread out.
When a substance is not concentrated, it is diluted or weak.
When energy is not concentrated, it is diffuse — spreading outward rather than being aimed at a point.
A Quick Note on Related Forms

Knowing these will help you recognize the word in the wild:

  • Concentrated (adjective): "Concentrated effort." "Concentrated orange juice." "A highly concentrated acid." — Describes something that has already been focused or strengthened.
  • Concentration (noun): "Her concentration was remarkable." "A high concentration of salt." "Troop concentration near the border." — The state or result of concentrating.
  • Concentrating (present participle): "He is concentrating on his work."

In short, "concentrate" is a word about intensity born from focus — pulling the scattered into the singular, and the weak into the powerful.
